I had this same thought, though I came at it from the other end. It started with the thought that we've begun to store our collective memories as purely digital content trusting that the Google servers or hard drive in our drawer will remain incorruptable for all of time. It hasn't happened completely yet, but that's the way it's been going. Until recently, hard copy family picture albums were in every home. Now a lot of people just keep all their photos on their phone.

Electronic data is more convenient but also ephemeral and more volatile. Imagine if China's Cultural Revolution took place in a world where most knowledge was stored digitally. You wouldn't have to root out all the books, carvings, and scrools and burn them in a massive bonfire. You'd just have to secure the server center and run an admin deletion command. Today, you can destroy a library's worth of book by snapping a microSD card in half.

It seems to me that the further a civ progresses on the non-phyiscal information storage route, the easier it is to wipe from history. Whether it's from natural disaster or socio-political upheavel, the threat just gets greater the more advanced a civilization gets. Larger structures might remain (pyramids? Hoover Dam?), but any finer tech would essentially evaporate from history leaving tales and legends.

Librarian/Archivist here: No.

One of the main roles played by a library or archives that's often overlooked is that they are the means by which people access information, and therefore have the power to oversee what information is available. Needless to say, this makes librarians a lot more damn powerful than they might seem at first glance.

If information is our gateway to history and truth, then whoever controls information serves as the gatekeepers. The most obvious of these gatekeepers is the government, but libraries (even public libraries) are also a key factor. Not just a means of restricting access further, either: When the USA PATRIOT Act was introduced, librarians devised means of working around it. (It should go without saying that pro-censorship librarians are rare.)

Libraries and archives help to ensure that history need not necessarily be written by the victors. If documents pertaining to Christopher Columbus were not properly preserved and archived, Howard Zinn would not have been able to conduct the research necessary to give the world another view of who he really was. Of course, librarians could let their own biases cloud their judgment of what is and is not worthy of preservation. I recently engaged in an argument with fellow archivists who were pushing for greater representation of "underrepresented communities" in archives. I felt that was the other side of the history-written-by-the-victors coin.

And even if all information is provided to the end user, librarians can still exert influence as to which information is seen and is taken as truth. In cataloging class ("LIS 415: Information Organization"), we discussed whether a children's book about dinosaurs from the perspective of creationists should be classified so that it's shelved in the science section. I declared that the debate boiled down to whether books should be classified according to the wishes of their authors. I claimed that if that were the case, I could write a book about how Richard Nixon assassinated JFK and have it placed alongside the legitimate history books. The question remained, of course, as to who would devise the criteria to determine whether information has merit. Presumably, that duty would fall to librarians.

If there were no humans to curate the flow of information, said information would be at the mercy of the powers that be. Governments and businesses could order the destruction of information as they pleased. Graphene SSDs and gigabit Internet won't matter much if there aren't people and institutions to manage, vet, and catalog the information they make available.
